question.problem:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $\frac{1}{4},\,\frac{1}{2},\,2,\,…$

II. ${a}_{n+1}=\frac{3}{2}{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=-1,\,n\ge 1$

III. $1,\,0.2,\,0.03,\,…$
question.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not a geometric sequence because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{1}{4})} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{2})} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is a geometric sequence. The recursive rule ${a}_{n+1}=\frac{3}{2}{a}_{n}$ tells us that each term is $\frac{3}{2}$ times the previous term, so the common ratio is $r=\frac{3}{2}.$

- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{0.2}{1} & =0.2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{0.03}{0.2} & =0.15\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence II is a geometric sequence.
